findings.message: Phase 7 explicitly promises the first-contact integrity ceremony payload is 'written out here verbatim as the shipped template', but the draft ends abruptly at 'before executing any file from the clone)' without providing the actual git/gpg commands. A missing root of trust violates the 'safe to run' criterion, as collaborators have no actionable way to verify the clone before execution.

Step 6 of the update transaction runs 'npm ci' on the collaborator's machine. If the shipped lockfile includes native dependencies, this step will reliably fail on pristine OS installs (especially Windows) lacking C++ build toolchains like MSVC or Xcode. This violates the 'working instance' criterion, as collaborators would be permanently locked out of updates and roll back endlessly without manual toolchain intervention.

The interactive bootstrap serves the claim nonce in the DOM of the /onboard page. A malicious browser extension with host permissions can read this nonce and execute the same-origin POST to /claim, capturing the session cookie. This violates the 'safe to expose' criterion by allowing a local extension to bypass the OS peer-credential identity check.

The distribution topology relies on a git clone of a release repo to receive the bundle, but Windows does not ship with git by default. A collaborator cannot run the preflight doctor without first acquiring the repo, violating the 'self-contained bundle' criterion by introducing an unstated, manual tool prerequisite prior to first contact.

The exposure matrix mandates the custom `X-Anchor-Request: 1` header on 'EVERY route + WS upgrade' as a CSRF defense. However, the browser's native `WebSocket` constructor does not support appending custom HTTP headers during the handshake. Enforcing this on the WebSocket upgrade route will categorically break the frontend's ability to establish real-time connections. The upgrade route must rely on the `Origin` header and session cookie, or use a ticket-based protocol.

The Secret Inventory strictly confines the master token: 'never leaves the engine process and its mode-0600 file'. However, operator CLI commands like `anchor claim`, `anchor pair`, and `anchor token rotate` run as separate processes and must communicate with the persistent engine daemon to arm claim windows or invalidate sessions. Because these CLI processes have no session cookie and are explicitly barred from holding the master token in their process memory, they possess no defined mechanism to authenticate their loopback API requests to the daemon.

Step 6 offline rollback executes 'delete the partial node_modules' before restoring the snapshot. On Windows, if `npm ci` was interrupted while a postinstall script left a background process holding a file handle inside `node_modules` (or if an AV scanner is holding a handle), directory deletion via `fs.rm` will fail with EBUSY/EPERM. Because the Phase 2 contention bound only explicitly covers `rename`, a failed deletion here will crash the rollback itself, violating the 'ALWAYS terminates in a working state' guarantee.

Phase 6 skill-integrity hashes enforce 'skills read-only / foundry-only-edit' via a 'documented foundry path for legitimate updates'. If a collaborator legitimately updates a skill, their local hash manifest is modified. During a Phase 4 update that brings new upstream hashes, the auto-stash will inevitably conflict on this manifest. The update transaction's 'Conflicting apply -> park-with-report' behavior will park the stash, effectively overwriting the collaborator's custom skills with upstream defaults on every update.

The headless SSH onboarding recipe rigidly pins the local forwarded port to the server's port to satisfy the Origin allowlist. If the collaborator's local machine already has a service bound to that port (e.g., 8080 or 3000), the SSH tunnel will fail to bind, and the user cannot complete the pairing process without either killing their local service or manually changing the server port (which violates the 'zero manual token handling/zero operator-typed git' smooth UX requirement).

The first-contact trust ceremony requires the collaborator to verify signed tags using 'their OWN locally-installed git/gpg' before executing any code from the clone. Because pristine Windows and macOS VMs do not include GPG by default, the onboarding flow deadlocks at step zero with a 'command not found' error. The user cannot even run `anchor doctor` to get installation instructions because running the doctor requires trusting the clone first.

The OS peer-credential check relies on TCP table lookups to ensure the browser and engine share an OS user. However, for a standard workflow where the engine runs in WSL and the browser runs on the Windows host, the connection crosses a proxy/forwarder boundary. The peer lookup inside WSL will see the forwarder process (often running as root), mismatch the engine user, and fail closed. This forces all WSL users into the fallback headless pairing path on their local machine, a significant UX degradation.

The update transaction automatically restores stashed working-tree edits (step 7) but merely parks locally diverged commits (step 2) and leaves them parked, requiring the operator to manually run `anchor edits restore` after every single update. This creates a deeply frustrating UX that punishes the operator for properly committing their local tweaks (by forcing manual restoration) while rewarding a dirty working tree (which auto-restores).

A missing root of trust violates the 'safe to run' criterion, as collaborators have no actionable way to verify the clone before execution.
